task_row_model.query: I need a production-quality, lock-free multiple-producer multiple-consumer (MPMC) queue in C++ for low-latency messaging between threads. Explain the Michael-Scott algorithm, provide clear enqueue/dequeue pseudocode using std::atomic and appropriate memory_order, discuss how to handle ABA and safe memory reclamation (hazard pointers or epoch-based reclamation), and note complexity and linearizability guarantees. Also mention common pitfalls when adapting this to real code.

documents.content: A typical thread-pool design separates task submission from execution using a bounded work queue per worker or a global queue with work-stealing. Workers pop tasks and execute them; the scheduler balances load by moving tasks between queues. Key considerations are minimizing contention on the global queue, amortizing task submission cost, and avoiding blocking in workers. For low-latency systems, prefer per-worker queues with occasional global balancing, use lock-free or low-contention rings for hot paths, and instrument queue lengths to make scheduling decisions. Backpressure and graceful shutdown must ensure no task is dropped and in-flight tasks complete before teardown.
documents.reasoning_trace: Summarized common thread-pool designs and trade-offs for low-latency task scheduling.

documents.content: Dmitry Vyukov's bounded MPMC queue uses a fixed-size ring buffer with per-slot sequence numbers to provide a wait-free enqueue/dequeue for multiple producers and consumers. Each slot holds a sequence counter; producers inspect slot.seq to see if it's available and then CAS the head index while setting the value and updating seq. Consumers similarly check seq to determine availability. This design is very cache-friendly and avoids dynamic allocation, but it requires a capacity chosen at construction (power-of-two usually) and cannot grow. It doesn’t address node reclamation because slots are reused; the algorithm is different from pointer-based lock-free queues with dynamic nodes.
documents.reasoning_trace: Condensed Vyukov's bounded ring algorithm focusing on sequence counters and bounded capacity; contrasted with dynamic pointer-based queues.

documents.content: Asynchronous file I/O and event completion systems use submission queues and completion rings to decouple I/O initiation from completion handling. Implementations maintain an event loop that polls or waits for completions, dispatches callbacks on threads, and may batch completions for throughput. Key points include avoiding busy-waits, using scalable notification primitives, and handling partial I/O and cancellation. For robustness, track outstanding operations and provide timeouts and cancellation paths. While important for high-throughput I/O systems, these mechanisms are orthogonal to in-memory lock-free data structures for inter-thread messaging.
documents.reasoning_trace: Outlined typical async I/O event loop mechanisms and considerations for robustness.

documents.content: The canonical lock-free MPMC queue is the Michael‑Scott queue: a singly linked list with atomic head and tail pointers and a dummy node. Node { value, atomic<Node*> next }. Enqueue: allocate node->next = nullptr; loop: read tail and tail->next; if tail still tail and tail->next==nullptr, CAS tail->next from nullptr to node; then CAS tail to node (helping). Dequeue: loop: read head, tail, head->next; if head==tail and head->next==nullptr empty; else read value from head->next and CAS head to head->next. Use std::atomic<Node*> and compare_exchange_weak/strong with memory_order_acq_rel for successful CAS, memory_order_acquire for loads that observe pointers, and memory_order_release for stores. Linearizability: enqueue linearizes at link (tail->next CAS) and dequeue at head CAS. Both operations are O(1) amortized. ABA and reclamation: you must not free a removed node immediately; use hazard pointers or epoch-based reclamation so readers hold safe references before CAS. With hazard pointers, publish the pointer you read, validate it, perform CAS, then retire nodes and reclaim only when no hazard pointer references them. Common pitfalls: forgetting the dummy node, incorrect memory_order leading to subtle reordering bugs, freeing nodes too early (ABA), and assuming FIFO under contention without observing helping behaviors. For production C++ code, combine std::atomic for pointers, careful memory_order choices, and a tested reclamation scheme (hazard pointers or epoch GC).
documents.reasoning_trace: Assembled a concise, correct description of Michael-Scott queue semantics, pseudocode steps, memory ordering guidance, and safe reclamation options based on standard papers and best practices.

documents.content: A simple concurrent queue can be implemented with std::mutex and std::condition_variable. Enqueue locks the mutex, pushes to std::deque or std::queue, then notifies a waiting consumer. Dequeue waits on the condition variable until the queue is non-empty, pops the front, and returns the value. This approach is easy to reason about and avoids ABA and reclamation issues, but it incurs kernel transitions and blocking under contention, which can add tail latency. For low-latency, lock-free algorithms are preferred; for moderate throughput and simplicity, mutex-based queues are robust and simpler to maintain.
documents.reasoning_trace: Explained standard mutex+condition-variable queue approach and trade-offs versus lock-free solutions.
